lesson.title: Rows and Columns: Working with a List of Lists
lesson.summary: When every element of a list is itself a list of the same shape, you get a grid like structure of rows and columns that you index with two brackets.
lesson.body:
Nested lists become especially useful when every inner list represents the same kind of thing, such as a row in a table or a row on a game board. A list where every element is a list is often called a list of lists, and it is the standard way to represent two dimensional data in Python since the language has no separate grid or matrix type built in.

Picture a 3 by 3 grid of numbers. You can write it as a list of three inner lists, each one representing a row:

```python
grid = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
    [7, 8, 9]
]
print(grid[1][2])

for row in grid:
    print(row)
```

This prints:

```
6
[1, 2, 3]
[4, 5, 6]
[7, 8, 9]
```

grid[1] selects the second row, [4, 5, 6], and the second bracket, [2], selects the third value inside that row, which is 6. This row then column ordering, grid[row][col], is the standard convention for two dimensional indexing, so it is worth memorizing rather than guessing each time. The for loop afterward traverses the outer list one row at a time, and since each row is itself a list, print(row) shows the whole inner list on each line rather than a single number.

A list of lists hides a trap that is worth seeing now, because it becomes important again when you learn about copying lists. If you build a grid by repeating the same inner list object instead of creating fresh ones, every row secretly points to the same underlying list in memory.

```python
row = [0, 0, 0]
board = [row, row, row]
board[0][0] = 9
print(board)
```

This prints:

```
[[9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0]]
```

Even though the code only touched board[0][0], all three rows changed, because board[0], board[1], and board[2] are not three separate lists, they are three names for the exact same list object, the one stored in row. Changing it through any one of those names changes what all of them show. When you need genuinely independent rows, build each one separately, for example with a list comprehension like [[0, 0, 0] for _ in range(3)], which creates three distinct list objects instead of three references to one.
